To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the strength of goal commitment is determined by the interplay between fantasy and reality.

the self-regulatory process of contrasting fantasy with reality leads to strong commitment to pursue goals when people believe that the goal is attainable (e.g., favorable expectations), to weak commitment to pursue goals if they do not believe in the attainability of the goal (e.g., unfavorable expectations), and to moderate commitment if they are not aware of their expectations (i.e., no contrast).
people who contrast their fantasies about the future with present reality are more strongly committed to their goal than people who only fantasize about the future or only reflect present reality.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the self-regulatory process that turns free fantasies about the desired future into binding goals.
the question of how the mere fantasy about a desired future can become a binding goal.
the question of how people turn free fantasies about the desired future into binding goals.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the more a goal is perceived as being attainable, the higher will be the goal commitment.
the self-regulation of goal striving is a complex process in which the interplay of various cognitive, motivational, and behavioral factors plays a major role.

the self-regulatory processes of fantasizing about the future and reflecting on the present are not sufficient for the emergence of strong goal commitment, and that they are not necessary for the emergence of moderate goal commitment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

fantasy realization theory can explain how people turn free fantasies about the desired future into binding goals, how they maintain these goals, how they realize these goals, and how they adapt these goals to changing circumstances.
the process of self-regulating goal setting is more complex than is commonly assumed in the literature on goal setting.
fantasy-realization theory provides a parsimonious and integrative explanation of goal-setting processes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
people are not only able to fantasize about a better future, but also able to turn fantasies about the future, which are often free of any necessity to act, into goals that guide behavior.
people are more likely to act on their goals if they contrast them with reality.
the mere fantasy about a future goal can be sufficient to activate the use of expectations and to generate moderate commitment.
